                            UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                          NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                    RELATED CASE ORDER


        A Motion for Administrative Relief to Consider Whether Cases Should be Related or a
Sua Sponte Judicial Referral for Purpose of Determining Relationship (Civil L.R. 3-12) has been
filed. The time for filing an opposition or statement of support has passed. As the judge assigned
to case

       25-cv-10301-VC
       Woodard v. OpenAI, Inc.

        I find that the more recently filed case(s) that I have initialed below are related to the case
assigned to me, and such case(s) shall be reassigned to me. Any cases listed below that are not
related to the case assigned to me are referred to the judge assigned to the next-earliest filed case
for a related case determination.


Case            Title                              Related Not Related
25-cv-10312-AGT ZEBRALINE GROUP, LLC v. OPENAI L.P  VC

                                               ORDER

         The parties are instructed that all future filings in any reassigned case are to bear the
initials of the newly assigned judge immediately after the case number. Any case management
conference in any reassigned case will be rescheduled by the Court. The parties shall adjust the
dates for the conference, disclosures and report required by FRCivP 16 and 26 accordingly.
Unless otherwise ordered, any dates for hearing noticed motions are vacated and must be re-
noticed by the moving party before the newly assigned judge; any deadlines set by the ADR Local
Rules remain in effect; and any deadlines established in a case management order continue to
govern, except dates for appearance in court, which will be rescheduled by the newly assigned
judge.


Dated: January 14, 2026                        By:
                                                     Vince Chhabria
                                                     United States District Judge

1                                           INTRODUCTION
2
3                   Plaintiffs ZEBRALINE GROUP, LLC and MORGAN ROSS (“Plaintiffs”),

4    individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated, by and through Plaintiffs’ undersigned

5    counsel, bring this class action lawsuit against OPENAI L.P. and MIXPANEL, INC.

6    (“Defendants” or “OpenAI” or “Mixpanel”) and allege, based upon information and belief and

7    the investigation of Plaintiffs’ counsel, as follows:

8                                    NATURE OF THE ACTION

9    1. This is a class action arising from a data security incident in which an unauthorized actor

10      accessed Mixpanel, Inc.’s (“Mixpanel”) systems and exported datasets relating to Mixpanel’s

11      customers, including OpenAI, L.P. (“OpenAI”). As a result, personal and analytics data

12      associated with Plaintiff’s OpenAI API account—including name, email address,

13      approximate location, browser and operating system, referring websites, and OpenAI user

14      and/or organization identifiers—was exported from Mixpanel’s systems without

15      authorization.

16   2. Immediately following disclosure of the incident, malicious actors used the compromised

17      data to launch targeted social engineering attempts against Plaintiff’s business, including

18      fraudulent communications to an employee that leveraged the compromised data.

19   3. Plaintiff brings this action on behalf of himself and a class of similarly situated individuals

20      whose data was compromised due to Defendants’ failure to implement reasonable data

21      security measures, failure to vet and supervise third-party vendors, and failure to provide

22      adequate and timely notice

23


                                                  2
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
              Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1       Filed 12/01/25      Page 3 of 13




1

2                                                   PARTIES

3    4.   Plaintiffs Morgan D. Ross and Zebraline Group, LLC are citizens of California. Morgan D.

4         Ross maintains an OpenAI API account, and Zebraline Group, LLC also uses OpenAI’s

5         services. Plaintiffs received notice that information associated with their accounts was

6         included in the dataset exported from Mixpanel’s systems without authorization.

7    5. Defendant OpenAI, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership with its principal place of business

8         in San Francisco, California, and is therefore a citizen of Delaware and California. OpenAI

9         provides AI models, developer APIs, and related services nationwide

10   6. Defendant Mixpanel, Inc. is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in

11        San Francisco, California, and is therefore a citizen of Delaware and California. Mixpanel

12        provides analytics and telemetry services that track user interactions with websites and

13        applications, including OpenAI’s platform.

14


15                                  JURISDICTION AND VENUE
16

17   7. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under the Class Action Fairness Act, 28 U.S.C. §

18        1332(d), because the proposed class contains at least 100 members, the amount in

19        controversy exceeds $5,000,000 exclusive of interest and costs, and minimal diversity exists.

20   8. The Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendants because they reside and conduct

21        substantial business in this District, and a substantial portion of the events and omissions

22        giving rise to these claims occurred here.



                                                  3
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1      Filed 12/01/25      Page 4 of 13




1    9. Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391 because Defendants reside in this

2       District and a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claims occurred

3       here.


4                                   FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
5

6                    A. OpenAI’s Use of Mixpanel and Security Obligations
7    10. OpenAI provides API-based access to its AI models through its platform interface used by

8       Plaintiff.

9    11. OpenAI engaged Mixpanel to provide analytics for the OpenAI API platform. Mixpanel’s

10      scripts collected and stored information about users’ interactions with OpenAI’s platform,

11      including names, email addresses, approximate locations, browser and operating systems,

12      referring websites, and internal user and organization identifiers.

13   12. Reasonable information security programs require, among other things, vendor due diligence

14      and risk assessment, data minimization, robust contractual and technical safeguards,

15      monitoring and detection of unauthorized access, least-privilege access controls, and timely

16      incident response and notification.

17   13. Defendants failed to implement reasonable security controls and failed to adequately

18      supervise Mixpanel’s handling of data associated with Plaintiff’s and Class Members’

19      accounts.


20                               B. The Mixpanel Security Incident

21   14. On or about November 2025, Mixpanel determined that an attacker had gained unauthorized

22      access to a portion of its systems and exported datasets relating to its customers, including

23      OpenAI.
                                                4
                                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT           Document 1        Filed 12/01/25     Page 5 of 13




1    15. Mixpanel informed OpenAI that the exported data included personal and analytics

2       information associated with users of OpenAI’s API.

3    16. OpenAI received the affected datasets from Mixpanel and initiated an investigation into the

4       scope and impact of the incident.

5    17. On or about November 26–27, 2025, OpenAI notified Plaintiff and other affected users that

6       an attacker exported a dataset from Mixpanel’s systems containing profile and analytics

7       information associated with their OpenAI API accounts and warned that the information

8       could be used for phishing or social engineering.

9    18. The impacted information includes, for each affected API user: name supplied on the

10      account, email address, approximate city, state, and country of use, browser and operating

11      system, referring websites, and OpenAI organization and/or user identifiers.

12   19. The compromised data enables highly effective phishing and impersonation attempts because

13      it can be used to tailor communications to targets with convincing context.


14                         C. Plaintiff’s Experience and Resulting Harms

15   20. Plaintiff received OpenAI’s incident notice on or about November 26, 2025.

16   21. On the morning of November 27, 2025, Plaintiff’s employee reported receiving suspicious

17      calls and emails that appeared to be from Plaintiff but were not.

18   22. These fraudulent communications used personal and contextual details consistent with the

19      types of data compromised in the Mixpanel incident and followed shortly after the disclosure.

20   23. Plaintiff did not initiate the communications; they were attempts by third parties to

21      impersonate Plaintiff and obtain information from his employee.




                                                 5
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT           Document 1        Filed 12/01/25      Page 6 of 13




1    24. As a result of Defendants’ failures, Plaintiff has suffered and continues to suffer: exposure of

2       personal and analytics data; heightened risk of phishing, impersonation, and fraud; time spent

3       addressing and mitigating the incident; anxiety and emotional distress; and out-of-pocket

4       expenses related to mitigation and increased security.

5    25. The risk to Plaintiff and Class Members is ongoing. Once exposed, personal information can

6       be copied, circulated, and misused indefinitely.


7
8                                      CLASS ALLEGATIONS
9

10   26. Plaintiff brings this action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 on behalf of himself and

11      a proposed class defined as: All natural persons in the United States whose personal and/or

12      analytics data associated with an OpenAI API account was accessed, exfiltrated, or

13      compromised in the Mixpanel security incident disclosed in or about November 2025.

14   27. California Subclass: All members of the Class who reside in California.

15   28. Excluded from the Class and Subclass are Defendants and their officers and directors, the

16      Court and its staff, and any person who timely and validly requests exclusion.

17   29. The Class is so numerous that joinder is impracticable. On information and belief, thousands

18      of OpenAI API users nationwide were affected.

19   30. Common questions of law and fact predominate over any individualized questions, including:

20      whether Defendants owed duties to Plaintiff and the Class; whether Defendants failed to

21      implement reasonable security and vendor oversight; whether the incident was caused by

22      Defendants’ acts or omissions; whether Defendants’ conduct caused damages; and the

23      appropriate measure of damages and injunctive relief.


                                                 6
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
              Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1        Filed 12/01/25      Page 7 of 13




1    31. Plaintiff’s claims are typical of the Class because they arise from the same incident, involve

2       similar data, and are based on the same legal theories.

3    32. Plaintiff will fairly and adequately protect the interests of the Class. Plaintiff has no conflicts

4       with the Class and has retained experienced counsel.

5    33. A class action is superior to individual suits because it will promote judicial economy, avoid

6       inconsistent outcomes, and allow recovery for claims that would be economically infeasible

7       to litigate individually.


8                                        CAUSES OF ACTION
9                          Count I: Negligence (Against All Defendants)
10   34. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

11   35. Defendants owed Plaintiff and Class Members a duty to exercise reasonable care in

12   collecting, storing, processing, and securing their personal and analytics data; to implement

13   reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards; to limit the scope and sensitivity of

14   data shared with vendors; to conduct due diligence and oversight of vendors; and to timely

15   detect, respond to, and notify affected individuals of unauthorized access.

16   36. Defendants breached their duties by failing to implement and maintain reasonable security

17   measures; failing to adequately vet, contract with, and monitor Mixpanel; allowing unauthorized

18   access and exfiltration of Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ data; and failing to provide adequate

19   and timely notice.

20   37. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants’ negligence, Plaintiff and Class Members

21   suffered injury, including exposure of personal information, increased risk of fraud and identity



                                                  7
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT           Document 1       Filed 12/01/25     Page 8 of 13




1    theft, time and expenses for mitigation, loss of privacy, and other economic and non-economic

2    damages.


3

4         Count II: Invasion of Privacy / Intrusion Upon Seclusion (Against All
5                                     Defendants)
6    38. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

7    39. Plaintiff and Class Members had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their personal and

8    analytics information collected in connection with the use of OpenAI’s services.

9    40. Defendants’ acts and omissions enabled unauthorized third parties to obtain this information,

10   constituting a serious and offensive invasion of privacy that would be highly objectionable to a

11   reasonable person.

12   41. Plaintiff and Class Members suffered harm as a result and are entitled to damages and

13   appropriate equitable relief.


14                      Count III: Breach of Contract (Against OpenAI)
15   42. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

16   Plaintiff entered into a binding agreement with OpenAI governing his use of the OpenAI API

17   and related services. The agreement includes OpenAI’s commitments to implement and maintain

18   appropriate security measures and responsibly manage third-party vendors.

19   43. OpenAI breached the agreement by failing to implement and maintain reasonable security

20   and vendor oversight, allowing unauthorized access and exfiltration of Plaintiff’s and Class

21   Members’ data.


                                                8
                                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1       Filed 12/01/25   Page 9 of 13




1    44. Plaintiff and Class Members suffered damages as a result of OpenAI’s breach.


2                  Count IV: Breach of Implied Contract (Against OpenAI)
3    45. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

4    46. By providing personal information to OpenAI and using its services, Plaintiff and Class

5    Members entered into implied contracts whereby OpenAI agreed to use their information for

6    legitimate purposes and to protect it with reasonable care.

7    47. OpenAI breached these implied contracts by failing to use reasonable security measures and

8    by allowing the information to be exposed through inadequate vendor security.

9    Plaintiff and Class Members suffered damages as a result.


10                 Count V: Breach of Confidence (Against All Defendants)
11   48. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

12   Plaintiff and Class Members conveyed information to Defendants in confidence and reasonably

13   expected it would be maintained in confidence and protected from unauthorized access.

14   49. Defendants breached that confidence by failing to maintain appropriate safeguards and

15   permitting disclosure and exfiltration in the incident.

16   Plaintiff and Class Members suffered damages as a result.


17                 Count VI: Unjust Enrichment (Against All Defendants)
18   50. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.




                                                 9
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
            Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT           Document 1       Filed 12/01/25     Page 10 of 13




1    51. Defendants received benefits, including revenues and valuable data-driven insights, from

2    Plaintiff and Class Members while failing to invest and implement adequate security and vendor

3    oversight.

4    52. It would be unjust for Defendants to retain those benefits without compensating Plaintiff and

5    Class Members for the harms caused by Defendants’ acts and omissions.


6        Count VII: Declaratory and Injunctive Relief (Against All Defendants)
7    53. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

8    54. An actual controversy exists as to whether Defendants’ current security practices and vendor

9    oversight are adequate to protect Plaintiff’s and Class Members’ information.

10   55. Plaintiff seeks a declaration that Defendants’ security and vendor management practices were

11   and remain inadequate, and an injunction requiring Defendants to implement and maintain

12   industry-standard security measures and vendor risk management, including at a minimum:

13   56. Independent, annual third-party security audits and penetration testing of Defendants and key

14   vendors;

15   57. Implementation of least-privilege and zero-trust access controls across systems containing

16   personal data;

17   58. Data minimization and segregation to limit vendor exposure to only what is strictly

18   necessary;

19   59.Enhanced vendor due diligence, contractual security requirements, and continuous

20   monitoring;

21   60. Employee security training and phishing-resilience programs;
                                                10
                                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT       Document 1        Filed 12/01/25      Page 11 of 13




1    Prompt, clear, and comprehensive breach notifications, and

2    61. At least three years of credit monitoring, identity-theft protection, and dark web monitoring

3    for affected individuals.


4

5                 Count VIII: Violation of California Unfair Competition Law
6               (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq.) (Against All Defendants)
7    62. Plaintiff realleges and incorporates the preceding paragraphs.

8    63. Defendants’ conduct as alleged herein constitutes unlawful, unfair, and/or fraudulent business

9    acts and practices within the meaning of California Business and Professions Code section 17200

10   et seq.

11   64. Defendants’ acts and omissions are “unlawful” under the UCL because they violate

12   California Civil Code section 1798.81.5 and other state and federal statutes and common-law

13   duties requiring reasonable data security and vendor oversight, and because the same conduct

14   that constitutes negligence, invasion of privacy, breach of contract, breach of implied contract,

15   breach of confidence, and unjust enrichment also constitutes “unlawful” business practices.

16   65. Defendants’ acts and omissions are “unfair” under the UCL because, among other things,

17   they unreasonably exposed Plaintiff and Class Members to a heightened risk of phishing,

18   impersonation, and fraud; failed to implement and maintain reasonable administrative, technical,

19   and physical safeguards; failed to reasonably vet and supervise Mixpanel; and shifted the costs

20   and burdens of the incident onto Plaintiff and Class Members. The gravity of these harms to

21   Plaintiff and Class Members outweighs any countervailing benefits to Defendants or




                                                 11
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1        Filed 12/01/25       Page 12 of 13




1    competition, and such harms could have been reasonably avoided through readily available

2    security and vendor-risk management measures.

3    66. To the extent Defendants made or disseminated statements— including in privacy policies,

4    security statements, or other public-facing materials— that reasonably led Plaintiff and Class

5    Members to believe their information would be protected with appropriate care and not exposed

6    through inadequate vendor security, Defendants’ practices were also “fraudulent” within the

7    meaning of the UCL because such statements were likely to deceive reasonable consumers and

8    account holders.

9    67. As a direct and proximate result of Defendants’ unlawful, unfair, and/or fraudulent business

10   practices, Plaintiff and Class Members have suffered injury in fact and lost money or property,

11   including but not limited to loss of the benefit of their bargains, loss of the value of their data,

12   out-of-pocket expenses, and time and resources spent responding to and mitigating the

13   consequences of the incident.

14   68. Plaintiff, on behalf of himself and the Class (and California Subclass), seeks restitution and

15   disgorgement of all monies wrongfully obtained by Defendants through their unlawful, unfair,

16   and/or fraudulent practices, as well as injunctive and declaratory relief to prevent the

17   continuation or recurrence of such practices. The injunctive relief described in Count VII is also

18   sought as a remedy under the UCL. Plaintiff also seeks attorneys’ fees and costs as permitted by

19   law, including under California Code of Civil Procedure section 1021.5


20                                      PRAYER FOR RELIEF

21   69. WHEREFORE, Plaintiff, individually and on behalf of the Class and Subclass, requests that

22   the Court enter judgment in his favor and against Defendants, and grant the following relief:
                                                    12
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-10312-AGT            Document 1        Filed 12/01/25     Page 13 of 13




1    70. Certify the Class and Subclass, appoint Plaintiff as Class Representative, and appoint

2    Plaintiff’s counsel as Class Counsel;

3    71. Award compensatory, consequential, and general damages in an amount to be proven at trial;

4    72. Award restitution and/or disgorgement to prevent Defendants’ unjust enrichment;

5    73. Enter declaratory and injunctive relief requiring implementation and maintenance of

6    adequate security and vendor oversight measures, and requiring provision of credit monitoring,

7    identity-theft protection, and related services to Plaintiff and Class Members;

8    74. Award pre- and post-judgment interest at the maximum rate permitted by law;

9    75. Award attorneys’ fees and costs as permitted by law; and

10   76. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

11   77. Plaintiff demands a trial by jury on all issues so triable.

12   78. Dated: November 29, 2025
13

14   Respectfully submitted,

15
16
17
18
